title: Best Vitelliform Macular Dystrophy (BVMD)
summary: A progressive, autosomal dominant macular dystrophy caused by mutations in the BEST1 gene, characterized by the accumulation of subretinal lipofuscin in a classic 'egg-yolk' appearance. It is uniquely identified by a pathognomonic reduction in the EOG Arden ratio despite a normal ERG.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Best Vitelliform Macular Dystrophy (BVMD), or 'Best Disease', is an autosomal dominant generalized tapetoretinal dystrophy. It primarily affects the Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE) and secondarily involves the photoreceptors. The hallmark is the bilateral, symmetrical accumulation of yellowish, 'egg-yolk' like material (lipofuscin) within the subretinal space, typically appearing in the first or second decade of life.

sections.title: Epidemiology & Genetics
content: Inheritance: Autosomal Dominant with variable expressivity and high penetrance.
Gene: BEST1 (formerly VMD2) located on chromosome 11q12.3.
Protein: Bestrophin-1, a transmembrane protein acting as a calcium-sensitive chloride channel in the RPE basolateral membrane.
Prevalence: Estimated at 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 15,000.
Age of Onset: Usually 3–15 years, though often asymptomatic until later stages.

sections.title: Pathophysiology Flow
content: Mutation in BEST1 gene → Defective Bestrophin-1 protein.
Impaired chloride ion transport across RPE basolateral membrane.
Failure of fluid regulation and phagocytosis in the subretinal space.
Accumulation of lipofuscin/vitelliform material (A2E) between RPE and photoreceptors.
Secondary RPE atrophy and photoreceptor degeneration.

rows: Normal fundus; abnormal EOG is the only finding.
Subtle RPE pigmentary changes or tiny yellow flecks.
Partial absorption of material; layer of yellow fluid settles inferiorly.
'Scrambled Egg' appearance as material breaks up.
Central RPE and chorioretinal atrophy; looks like GA.

content.explanation: In Best Disease, the EOG (Electro-oculogram) is ALWAYS abnormal. The Arden Ratio (Light peak / Dark trough) is typically < 1.5 (Normal > 1.85). CRITICALLY: The Full-field ERG remains NORMAL because the global photoreceptor function is preserved.

branches: OCT: Hyperreflective material between RPE and Ellipsoid Zone
FAF: Intense hyper-autofluorescence of vitelliform material
FFA: Early blockage (masking) by material; late staining
OCT-A: Used to rule out CNV in stage 6

rows: Smaller lesions, older age (40-60), minimal progression.
Pisciform flecks, 'dark choroid' on FFA, early vision loss.
Serous detachment without yellow material; 'smoke stack' FFA.
History of sun gazing, small foveal hole/defect.
Pigment at RPE level, various patterns (butterfly, etc.).

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: Step 1: Baseline EOG and Genetic testing (BEST1).
Step 2: Annual monitoring with OCT and Amsler Grid.
Step 3: Screen family members (even if asymptomatic) with EOG.
Step 4: Treat CNV (Stage 6) with intravitreal Anti-VEGF (e.g., Ranibizumab, Aflibercept).
Step 5: Low vision rehabilitation for atrophic stages.

sections.title: Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: Sudden drop in vision or new metamorphopsia (Suggests CNV).
Subretinal hemorrhage or hard exudates on fundoscopy.
Rapidly expanding subretinal fluid on OCT.
Development of Macular Hole (Rare complication of stage 4/5).

content.explanation: Pre-vitelliform, Vitelliform (Yolk), Pseudohypopyon, Vitelliruptive (Scrambled), Atrophic, Cicatricial.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: Vision often remains surprisingly good despite a dramatic 'egg-yolk' appearance.
An abnormal EOG in a parent with a normal fundus confirms they are a carrier.
The vitelliform material is located between the RPE and the photoreceptors (subretinal).
Anti-VEGF response for CNV in Best disease is generally very good.

sections.title: Recent Advances
sections.content: Gene therapy is the most promising frontier for BVMD. Ongoing research focuses on adeno-associated virus (AAV) mediated delivery of a functional BEST1 gene to the RPE. Recent studies using patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) have successfully modeled the chloride channel defect and tested potential small-molecule therapies to enhance RPE function.
